Race Conditions.subject: OS
Race Conditions.overview: A race condition occurs in concurrent execution when multiple processes or threads access shared resources simultaneously without adequate synchronization, leading to unpredictable outcomes.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Race condition
resources.description: Comprehensive overview of race conditions, critical sections, and formal definitions.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Mutual exclusion
resources.description: Explains mutual exclusion principles, algorithms, and hardware support.

resources.title: Python Docs: Thread Synchronization Primitives
resources.description: Standard documentation for Locks, RLocks, and Semaphores.

subparts.title: Critical Section Problem
subparts.summary: The critical section is code accessing shared data. Synchronization must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting to prevent state corruption.
learning_goals: Identify critical sections in concurrent code
Explain the three requirements for critical section solutions

subparts.title: Atomic Operations & Hardware Primitives
subparts.summary: Hardware instructions like Test-and-Set and Compare-and-Swap execute atomically. These primitives form the bedrock of spinlocks and modern lock-free data structures.
learning_goals: Understand Test-and-Set and CAS primitives
Analyze how atomic instructions eliminate race windows

subparts.title: Mutexes & Spinlocks
subparts.summary: Mutex locks provide boolean locking where threads sleep if the lock is held. Spinlocks busy-wait, making them suitable only for very short waits on multiprocessors.
learning_goals: Compare mutex sleeping versus spinlock busy-waiting
Evaluate lock contention and overhead in multi-threaded programs

subparts.title: Deadlock and Priority Inversion
subparts.summary: Poor lock acquisition orders can induce deadlocks. Priority inversion occurs when a low-priority thread holding a lock blocks a high-priority thread, solved by priority inheritance.
learning_goals: Diagnose priority inversion scenarios
Explain priority inheritance protocols

subparts.title: Lock-Free Programming & Memory Barriers
subparts.summary: Lock-free algorithms use memory barriers and atomic instructions to coordinate without mutexes. Compilers and CPUs can reorder instructions unless fenced.
learning_goals: Understand memory fences and happens-before relations
Distinguish lock-free versus wait-free progress guarantees

Deadlocks.subject: OS
Deadlocks.overview: A deadlock is a state where each member of a set of processes is waiting for an event that only another member in the set can cause.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Deadlock (computer science)
resources.description: Formal definitions of deadlocks, Coffman conditions, and mitigation strategies.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Banker's algorithm
resources.description: Detailed explanation of Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm for deadlock avoidance.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Dining philosophers problem
resources.description: Classic synchronization problem illustrating deadlocks and resource allocation.

subparts.title: The Four Coffman Conditions
subparts.summary: Deadlocks require mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Breaking any one condition guarantees that a deadlock cannot occur.
learning_goals: State and explain the four Coffman conditions
Analyze systems to detect vulnerable resource allocations

subparts.title: Resource Allocation Graphs (RAG)
subparts.summary: Directed graphs model resource requests and assignments. A cycle in a single-instance resource graph indicates a deadlock, whereas multi-instance graphs require matrix reduction.
learning_goals: Construct and trace Resource Allocation Graphs
Identify cycles and knot conditions indicating deadlock

subparts.title: Deadlock Prevention vs Avoidance
subparts.summary: Prevention structurally invalidates one of the Coffman conditions. Avoidance uses runtime knowledge of future resource demands (e.g. Banker's Algorithm) to stay in safe states.
learning_goals: Distinguish static prevention from dynamic avoidance
Evaluate trade-offs in resource utilization and concurrency

subparts.title: Banker's Algorithm & Safe States
subparts.summary: A state is safe if there exists an execution sequence allowing all processes to complete. The Banker's Algorithm checks if granting a request leaves the system in a safe state.
learning_goals: Execute the Safety Algorithm on allocation matrices
Determine whether resource requests should be granted or delayed

subparts.title: Deadlock Detection & Recovery
subparts.summary: Detection algorithms periodically search for cycles or deadlocked states. Recovery strategies include process termination (aborting all or one by one) and resource preemption.
learning_goals: Implement wait-for graph cycle detection
Choose optimal victim processes for termination or rollback

Semaphores.subject: OS
Semaphores.overview: A semaphore is a synchronization variable initialized to an integer that coordinates access to shared resources via atomic wait (P) and signal (V) operations.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Semaphore (programming)
resources.description: Historical context, Dijkstra's formulation, and counting vs binary semaphores.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Producer-consumer problem
resources.description: Standard bounded buffer coordination using counting and binary semaphores.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Readers-writers problem
resources.description: Concurrent read and exclusive write synchronization patterns.

subparts.title: Counting vs Binary Semaphores
subparts.summary: Binary semaphores take values 0 or 1 to provide mutual exclusion. Counting semaphores track a pool of available resources, decrementing on wait and incrementing on signal.
learning_goals: Understand atomic wait() and signal() mechanics
Choose between binary and counting semaphores

subparts.title: Producer-Consumer (Bounded Buffer)
subparts.summary: Coordinating producers and consumers requires three semaphores: a mutex for buffer access, 'empty' slots, and 'full' slots to prevent underflow and overflow.
learning_goals: Implement bounded-buffer synchronization
Trace producer and consumer interleavings without race conditions

subparts.title: Readers-Writers Problem
subparts.summary: Multiple readers can access data simultaneously, but writers require exclusive access. Priority policies balance reader throughput against writer starvation.
learning_goals: Model reader-preference and writer-preference solutions
Prevent thread starvation in high-throughput data stores

subparts.title: Dining Philosophers Synchronization
subparts.summary: Philosophers alternating between eating and thinking demonstrate deadlock and starvation. Solutions include asymmetric pickup, resource hierarchy, and monitors.
learning_goals: Formulate deadlock-free chopstick acquisition
Analyze fairness and progress guarantees

subparts.title: Monitors & Condition Variables
subparts.summary: Monitors encapsulate shared data and synchronization in high-level language constructs. Condition variables provide explicit wait and signal signaling within monitors.
learning_goals: Compare low-level semaphores with high-level monitors
Understand Hoare versus Mesa monitor signaling semantics

Paging and Virtual Memory.subject: OS
Paging and Virtual Memory.overview: Virtual memory decouples logical process address spaces from physical RAM using paging, translation lookaside buffers (TLBs), and page fault handling.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Virtual memory
resources.description: Comprehensive reference on virtual address spaces, page tables, and memory hierarchy.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Page table
resources.description: Structure of multi-level, inverted, and hashed page tables.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Page replacement algorithm
resources.description: Evaluation of FIFO, LRU, LFU, and optimal Belady algorithms.

subparts.title: Paging & Address Translation
subparts.summary: Logical addresses are split into page numbers and offsets. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates page numbers into frame numbers using page tables.
learning_goals: Calculate page and offset bits from address widths
Translate logical addresses to physical addresses

subparts.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
subparts.summary: The TLB is a high-speed hardware cache for page table translations. High TLB hit ratios are essential to avoid multi-memory-access penalties per instruction.
learning_goals: Calculate effective memory access times (EMAT)
Explain TLB misses, flushes, and ASID tagging

subparts.title: Multi-Level & Inverted Page Tables
subparts.summary: 64-bit address spaces require hierarchical page tables to avoid storing gigantic linear tables in RAM. Inverted page tables map physical frames back to processes.
learning_goals: Design multi-level page table tree structures
Evaluate memory overhead of hierarchical versus inverted tables

subparts.title: Page Faults & Demand Paging
subparts.summary: When an access touches a non-present page, the MMU triggers a page fault exception. The OS fetches the required page from swap and updates the page table.
learning_goals: Trace the complete step-by-step page fault lifecycle
Analyze disk I/O latency impact on instruction restart

subparts.title: Page Replacement Algorithms & Thrashing
subparts.summary: When frames are full, replacement policies (FIFO, LRU, Clock, Belady's Optimal) select victim pages. Thrashing occurs when processes spend more time paging than executing.
learning_goals: Simulate LRU, FIFO, and Clock replacement algorithms
Identify Belady's anomaly and calculate working sets

CPU Scheduling.subject: OS
CPU Scheduling.overview: CPU scheduling determines which ready process is allocated the CPU, balancing throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and responsiveness.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Scheduling (computing)
resources.description: Overview of scheduling algorithms, preemptive vs non-preemptive paradigms, and metrics.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Round-robin scheduling
resources.description: Detailed look at round-robin time-slicing and responsiveness tradeoffs.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Multilevel feedback queue
resources.description: Adaptive scheduling with priority queues and dynamic aging.

subparts.title: Scheduling Criteria & Metrics
subparts.summary: Schedulers optimize turnaround time, waiting time, response time, and CPU utilization. Preemptive algorithms interrupt executing processes; non-preemptive algorithms run until burst completion.
learning_goals: Define core scheduling performance metrics
Differentiate preemptive versus cooperative scheduling

subparts.title: First-Come, First-Served & Convoy Effect
subparts.summary: FCFS executes processes in arrival order. A long CPU-bound process blocks short I/O-bound processes, causing low device utilization known as the convoy effect.
learning_goals: Draw Gantt charts for FCFS schedules
Explain and mitigate the convoy effect

subparts.title: Shortest Job First & Shortest Remaining Time
subparts.summary: SJF minimizes average waiting time by selecting the smallest CPU burst. Preemptive SJF (SRTF) immediately switches to newly arriving shorter jobs.
learning_goals: Prove SJF optimality for average waiting time
Estimate next burst duration using exponential smoothing

subparts.title: Round Robin & Quantum Tuning
subparts.summary: Round Robin allocates each process a fixed time slice (quantum). A large quantum degenerates into FCFS, while a very small quantum causes excessive context-switch overhead.
learning_goals: Select optimal time quantum values based on context switch costs
Calculate turnaround time under round-robin scheduling

subparts.title: Multi-Level Feedback Queues (MLFQ)
subparts.summary: MLFQ uses multiple priority queues with decreasing time quanta. Processes that consume their full quantum drop to lower queues; aging elevates starving processes.
learning_goals: Understand MLFQ heuristic priority adjustment
Implement aging to prevent process starvation

Transactions.subject: DBMS
Transactions.overview: A transaction is an atomic unit of database processing that transitions data from one consistent state to another, governed by ACID properties.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Database transaction
resources.description: Comprehensive reference for transaction semantics, ACID, and concurrency control.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Two-phase locking
resources.description: Formal proof and details of 2PL ensuring serializability.

resources.title: PostgreSQL Docs: Concurrency Control & Isolation
resources.description: Production PostgreSQL guide to Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) and transaction isolation.

subparts.title: ACID Properties
subparts.summary: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing execution. Consistency preserves integrity constraints, Isolation prevents concurrent interference, and Durability guarantees committed changes persist.
learning_goals: Define each ACID property in detail
Explain the database mechanisms that enforce each property

subparts.title: Schedules & Serializability
subparts.summary: Concurrent transactions produce interleaved schedules. A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations.
learning_goals: Construct precedence graphs to test conflict serializability
Distinguish view serializability from conflict serializability

subparts.title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
subparts.summary: 2PL requires a growing phase where locks are acquired and a shrinking phase where locks are released. Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, preventing cascading rollbacks.
learning_goals: Apply 2PL rules to transaction schedules
Explain why Strict and Rigorous 2PL prevent cascading aborts

subparts.title: Isolation Levels & Anomalies
subparts.summary: SQL isolation levels trade isolation for performance: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms.
learning_goals: Identify dirty reads, unrepeatable reads, and phantom phenomena
Map SQL standard isolation levels to concurrency phenomena

subparts.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) & Recovery
subparts.summary: WAL mandates that log records must be flushed to disk before corresponding database pages. ARIES recovery applies analysis, redo, and undo passes to recover state after crashes.
learning_goals: Understand the Write-Ahead Logging protocol
Trace ARIES checkpoint analysis, redo, and undo passes

Normalization.subject: DBMS
Normalization.overview: Database normalization organizes relational schema to minimize data redundancy and eliminate insert, update, and delete anomalies using functional dependencies.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Database normalization
resources.description: Formal definitions of 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, and dependency preservation.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Boyce–Codd normal form
resources.description: Detailed mathematical criteria and decomposition algorithms for BCNF.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Third normal form
resources.description: Codd's definition of 3NF eliminating transitive dependencies.

subparts.title: Functional Dependencies & Armstrong's Axioms
subparts.summary: A functional dependency X -> Y means X uniquely determines Y. Armstrong's Axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) allow computing attribute closures and candidate keys.
learning_goals: Compute the attribute closure of an attribute set
Derive all candidate keys for a given relation

subparts.title: First, Second, and Third Normal Forms
subparts.summary: 1NF requires atomic attribute values. 2NF removes partial key dependencies. 3NF removes transitive dependencies, ensuring non-prime attributes depend only on the primary key.
learning_goals: Identify modification anomalies in unnormalized schemas
Decompose relations into 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF

subparts.title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
subparts.summary: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey. BCNF strictly eliminates all functional redundancy, though it may sacrifice dependency preservation.
learning_goals: Verify whether a relation is in BCNF
Decompose relations into BCNF using closure analysis

subparts.title: Lossless Join & Dependency Preservation
subparts.summary: Decomposition must be lossless so that the natural join of decomposed relations reproduces the original relation exactly. Preserving dependencies avoids costly multi-table constraint checks.
learning_goals: Test decompositions for lossless-join property
Evaluate whether functional dependencies are preserved after decomposition

subparts.title: Denormalization & Query Optimization
subparts.summary: High normal forms introduce joins that can slow down read-heavy workloads. Pragmatic database design selectively denormalizes tables to optimize read performance while managing write overhead.
learning_goals: Identify when denormalization is justified in production databases
Analyze tradeoffs between storage redundancy and query response time

Indexing.subject: DBMS
Indexing.overview: Database indexing creates auxiliary data structures (B-trees, B+ trees, hash indexes) that accelerate data retrieval at the cost of storage and write overhead.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Database index
resources.description: Comprehensive reference covering primary, secondary, clustered, and dense indexes.

resources.title: Wikipedia: B+ tree
resources.description: Details the leaf-linked tree structure ideal for disk blocks and range queries.

resources.title: PostgreSQL Docs: Indexes
resources.description: Official guide to B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, and BRIN index implementations.

subparts.title: Index Structures: Clustered vs Non-Clustered
subparts.summary: A clustered index dictates the physical storage order of data rows on disk, meaning a table can have only one. Non-clustered indexes store pointers back to table rows.
learning_goals: Differentiate clustered and non-clustered index layouts
Evaluate query performance for range versus point lookups

subparts.title: B-Trees and B+ Trees
subparts.summary: B+ trees store data pointers exclusively in leaf nodes and link leaves sequentially. This provides logarithmic lookups, predictable tree depth, and optimal range scans on disk.
learning_goals: Trace search, insert, and node splitting in B+ trees
Calculate tree height and fanout based on disk page size

subparts.title: Hash Indexes vs Tree Indexes
subparts.summary: Hash indexes offer O(1) point lookups using bucket arrays but cannot support range queries or sorting. Tree indexes provide O(log N) operations and efficiently support range scans.
learning_goals: Compare hash indexing against B+ tree indexing
Select the appropriate index type based on workload access patterns

subparts.title: Composite & Covering Indexes
subparts.summary: Composite indexes index multiple columns in order; queries must match the leftmost prefix. A covering index contains all columns requested by a query, avoiding table lookups entirely.
learning_goals: Apply the leftmost prefix rule in multi-column indexes
Design covering indexes to eliminate disk page fetches

subparts.title: Index Maintenance & Write Amplification
subparts.summary: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE requires updating corresponding indexes, causing write amplification and page splits. Unused indexes degrade write throughput without providing read benefit.
learning_goals: Measure index overhead on write operations
Analyze database query plans using EXPLAIN to spot index usage

SQL Joins.subject: DBMS
SQL Joins.overview: SQL joins combine columns from one or more tables based on related keys, using algorithms like nested loops, hash joins, and sort-merge joins.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Join (SQL)
resources.description: Comprehensive reference covering inner, outer, cross, and self joins.

resources.title: PostgreSQL Documentation: Table Expressions & Joins
resources.description: Official PostgreSQL reference on join syntax, execution semantics, and lateral joins.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Relational algebra
resources.description: Mathematical foundations of natural joins, theta joins, and Cartesian products.

subparts.title: Inner vs Outer Joins
subparts.summary: Inner joins return only rows with matches in both tables. Outer joins (LEFT, RIGHT, FULL) preserve unmatched rows from one or both tables, populating missing columns with NULL.
learning_goals: Write queries using INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER joins
Predict NULL handling in outer join filtering conditions

subparts.title: Cross Joins & Self Joins
subparts.summary: Cross joins produce the Cartesian product of two tables. Self joins join a table to itself using table aliases to model hierarchical data such as organizational charts.
learning_goals: Construct self-joins to query hierarchical data
Estimate result set cardinality of Cartesian cross joins

subparts.title: Nested Loop Join Algorithm
subparts.summary: Nested loop joins iterate over the outer table and probe the inner table for matching rows. Index nested loop joins achieve high efficiency when the inner table has an index.
learning_goals: Trace simple and index-assisted nested loop joins
Calculate disk block access costs for nested loop variants

subparts.title: Hash Joins
subparts.summary: Hash joins build an in-memory hash table on the smaller build input and scan the larger probe input. They excel at handling large, unsorted equijoins without index requirements.
learning_goals: Explain build and probe phases in hash joins
Analyze memory constraints and hybrid hash join partitioning

subparts.title: Sort-Merge Joins & Join Order Optimization
subparts.summary: Sort-merge joins sort both inputs on join keys and scan them simultaneously. Query optimizers use cost-based models to choose the most efficient join order and algorithm.
learning_goals: Trace sort-merge join execution on pre-sorted inputs
Interpret query plans to verify optimizer join selection

Dynamic Programming.subject: DSA
Dynamic Programming.overview: Dynamic programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, caching results via memoization or tabulation.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Dynamic programming
resources.description: Bellman's principle of optimality, overlapping subproblems, and formal mathematical foundation.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Memoization
resources.description: Technique of storing function call results to avoid redundant subproblem calculations.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Bellman equation
resources.description: Mathematical formulation of optimality conditions in dynamic programming.

subparts.title: Optimal Substructure & Overlapping Subproblems
subparts.summary: Dynamic programming applies when the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, and subproblems recur repeatedly rather than generating new subproblems.
learning_goals: Identify optimal substructure in algorithmic problems
Differentiate divide-and-conquer from dynamic programming

subparts.title: Top-Down Memoization vs Bottom-Up Tabulation
subparts.summary: Top-down memoization adds a cache to recursive calls, evaluating only reachable states. Bottom-up tabulation iteratively fills an array in topological dependency order.
learning_goals: Convert recursive solutions to memoized top-down code
Construct iterative bottom-up DP tables with correct base cases

subparts.title: Classic 1D DP: Fibonacci, Climbing Stairs & LIS
subparts.summary: 1D DP problems depend on a small constant number of previous states. Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) uses DP in O(N^2) or binary search patience sorting in O(N log N).
learning_goals: Formulate 1D state transitions and recurrence relations
Optimize 1D DP space complexity to O(1) auxiliary memory

subparts.title: Classic 2D DP: Knapsack & Longest Common Subsequence
subparts.summary: 0/1 Knapsack decisions (include or exclude item) depend on remaining capacity and available items. LCS matches character suffixes to find maximal common sequence lengths.
learning_goals: Construct 2D state transition matrices for bounded knapsacks
Trace and reconstruct solutions from DP tables

subparts.title: State Compression & Space Optimization
subparts.summary: When recurrence relations only access the previous row or column, space complexity can be reduced from O(N*M) to O(min(N, M)) using rolling arrays or bitmasks.
learning_goals: Apply rolling array techniques to optimize 2D DP space
Design bitmask representations for subset state tracking
